newsitem.title: JAPAN: Green Cross plans streamlining amid HIV turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Green Cross plans streamlining amid HIV turmoil.

text.p: Japanese pharmaceuticals maker Green Cross Corp, bracing for a severe blow to its earnings from a scandal over HIV-tainted products, is considering radical measures to prop itself up.

In late September, Green Cross said it expected sales for the half-year to September 30 to have totalled 36.5 billion yen ($320 million), down from its earlier outlook of 42 billion yen ($368 million).

The company says the bleak earnings prospects are due mainly to a scandal, which erupted earlier this year, concerning the sale of blood products which were contaminated with the AIDS-causing HIV virus by Green Cross and several other companies.
Public outrage over the scandal prompted boycotts of Green Cross's products at many medical institutions throughout Japan, and this has resulted in a sharp fall in the firm's sales.
Since July, monthly sales have reached only 80 percent of the company's target, a Green Cross spokesman said.

Also, Green Cross expects it will have to pay a total of about 25 billion yen ($219 million) as compensation to about 2,000 haemophiliacs and other patients who became infected with HIV through the company's blood products.
The company will announce steps aimed at rebuilding its business when it unveils its half-year earnings results on November 1, the company spokesman said.
The company has already announced some plans to streamline its operations.
In September, it said it plans to close two of its four plants in Japan by 2000, and that it would also reduce its workforce from the current 2,400 to 2,000 within three or four years.

The spokesman said, however, that the company feels it must carry out more far-reaching restructuring measures in view of the fact it has asked its main creditor bank Sakura Bank Ltd for financial assistance.
The pharmaceuticals maker has asked Sakura Bank to provide financial aid worth several billion yen (tens of millions of dollars) partly because it needed help for the compensation payments.
Despite the huge financial burden of the compensation payments and the decline in sales, the company is banking its hopes on its leading technology in developing and producing blood products.
Analysts said the company is still a major supplier of many necessary blood products.

Green Cross is also preparing to launch a new blood product to treat excessive bleeding as early as the end of 1999. The new product, developed with bio-technology, is recombinant-human serum albumin.
"The outlook for the future of Green Cross really depends on the profitability of the new product," said Mitsuo Ohmi, senior analyst at Smith Barney International Inc.
He also pointed out that the Ministry of Heath and Welfare plays a very important role in the firm's survival, because it decides the product's pricing in the national insurance sytem.
Green Cross plans to spend about 14 billion yen ($122 million) to build a new plant in Chitose in Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost island, to make the new product.
